antidotes.stem: A 30-year-old is brought in after a large bupropion XL overdose and has a generalised tonic–clonic seizure. Oxygenation and glucose are normal.
antidotes.explain: Benzodiazepines are **first-line for seizures** caused by bupropion toxicity; treat recurrent seizures with escalating anticonvulsant therapy and supportive care.
wrong: IV phenytoin
Phenytoin is generally ineffective for toxicological seizures and may worsen dysrhythmias.
Flumazenil
It reverses benzodiazepines, not bupropion toxicity, and can precipitate seizures.
Naloxone
It reverses opioid toxicity, not bupropion-induced seizures.

antidotes.stem: A patient presents after a citalopram overdose with recurrent torsades de pointes and a prolonged QT interval. They remain conscious between episodes.
antidotes.explain: IV **magnesium sulfate** is the acute treatment for torsades de pointes, even if the serum magnesium is normal.
wrong: IV calcium gluconate
Calcium is not the treatment for torsades caused by QT prolongation.
IV sodium bicarbonate
This is used for sodium-channel blockade with QRS widening, not isolated QT prolongation.
Adenosine
Adenosine treats selected supraventricular tachycardias, not torsades.

antidotes.stem: A patient has taken a large carbamazepine overdose and remains markedly drowsy, with a rising serum concentration and no ileus or bowel obstruction. The airway is protected.
antidotes.explain: Carbamazepine undergoes **enterohepatic recirculation**; multiple-dose activated charcoal can enhance elimination in significant poisoning when the airway is protected.
wrong: Flumazenil
It does not reverse carbamazepine toxicity and may provoke seizures.
Whole-bowel irrigation as the sole measure
It may be considered in selected cases, but multiple-dose activated charcoal is the specific enhanced-elimination treatment here.
Urinary alkalinisation
This does not meaningfully enhance carbamazepine elimination.
antidotes.source: TOXBASE: Carbamazepine overdose; AACT/EAPCCT position statement on multiple-dose activated charcoal

antidotes.stem: After a lamotrigine overdose, a patient develops hypotension and a markedly widened QRS complex on ECG. There is no evidence of hyperkalaemia.
antidotes.explain: Sodium bicarbonate is used for suspected **sodium-channel blockade with QRS widening** in severe lamotrigine poisoning.
wrong: IV magnesium sulfate
Magnesium is used for torsades, not QRS widening from sodium-channel blockade.
IV calcium gluconate
Calcium treats selected calcium-channel blocker toxicities and hyperkalaemia, not this ECG effect.
Flumazenil
It does not reverse lamotrigine toxicity and may precipitate seizures.
antidotes.source: TOXBASE: Lamotrigine overdose; Goldfrank’s Toxicologic Emergencies, 11th ed.

antidotes.stem: A patient with a quetiapine overdose remains hypotensive after initial fluid resuscitation. ECG shows sinus tachycardia without QRS widening.
antidotes.explain: If hypotension persists after fluids, **noradrenaline** is an appropriate vasopressor for quetiapine-associated vasodilatory hypotension.
wrong: IV propranolol
Beta-blockade may worsen hypotension and is not indicated for sinus tachycardia in this setting.
IV physostigmine
It is not routine treatment for quetiapine overdose and may cause serious adverse effects.
IV sodium bicarbonate
There is no QRS widening to indicate treatment for sodium-channel blockade.

antidotes.stem: Following a massive ibuprofen overdose, a patient develops severe high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis and haemodynamic compromise. The airway and circulation are being supported.
antidotes.right: IV sodium bicarbonate for severe metabolic acidosis
antidotes.explain: There is no specific antidote; **IV sodium bicarbonate** may be used to correct severe, clinically significant acidaemia alongside supportive care.
wrong: N-acetylcysteine
It is an antidote for paracetamol poisoning, not ibuprofen toxicity.
Urinary alkalinisation to enhance ibuprofen clearance
Alkalinisation is not an established method to enhance ibuprofen elimination.
Flumazenil
It has no role in NSAID poisoning.

antidotes.stem: A patient presents after an extended-release venlafaxine overdose and has a generalised seizure. Point-of-care glucose and oxygenation are normal.
antidotes.explain: Treat venlafaxine-related seizures promptly with a **benzodiazepine** and provide supportive airway and cardiorespiratory care.
wrong: IV phenytoin
Phenytoin is generally not recommended for seizures caused by drug poisoning.
Flumazenil
It does not treat venlafaxine toxicity and may precipitate seizures.
Naloxone
It is not an antidote for venlafaxine-induced seizures.
antidotes.source: TOXBASE: Venlafaxine overdose; Goldfrank’s Toxicologic Emergencies, 11th ed.

antidotes.stem: During a regional anaesthetic, a patient develops a seizure followed by ventricular arrhythmia shortly after receiving bupivacaine. Local anaesthetic systemic toxicity is suspected.
antidotes.explain: For severe **local anaesthetic systemic toxicity**, administer 20% lipid emulsion alongside resuscitation and seizure control.
wrong: Intravenous sodium bicarbonate
Used for sodium-channel blocker toxicity, not as the specific rescue treatment for bupivacaine toxicity.
Intravenous calcium gluconate
Does not reverse local anaesthetic systemic toxicity.
Intravenous naloxone
Reverses opioid toxicity, not bupivacaine toxicity.
antidotes.source: ASRA Checklist for Treatment of Local Anesthetic Systemic Toxicity, 2020

antidotes.stem: A patient accidentally takes a large daily dose of methotrexate instead of the prescribed weekly dose and develops mucositis and pancytopenia. The serum methotrexate concentration is elevated.
antidotes.explain: Leucovorin bypasses the folate blockade and is the key **rescue treatment** after methotrexate toxicity; dosing is guided by the exposure and clinical context.
wrong: Folic acid alone
It is not an adequate substitute for leucovorin rescue in significant methotrexate toxicity.
Uridine triacetate
This is an antidote for fluoropyrimidine toxicity, not methotrexate.
Methylene blue
Used for methaemoglobinaemia, not antifolate toxicity.
antidotes.source: NHS Specialist Pharmacy Service, Managing interactions with methotrexate; EXTRIP Workgroup, Methotrexate recommendations

antidotes.stem: A patient with end-stage kidney disease accidentally takes a large amount of gabapentin and becomes deeply obtunded, requiring mechanical ventilation. Gabapentin is predominantly renally eliminated.
antidotes.explain: In severe gabapentin poisoning with **impaired kidney function**, extracorporeal removal is suggested; provide supportive care as well.
wrong: Intravenous flumazenil
Gabapentin is not a benzodiazepine, and flumazenil will not reverse its effects.
Intravenous naloxone
Naloxone does not reverse gabapentin toxicity.
Activated charcoal as the sole treatment
It does not address severe established toxicity or impaired drug clearance.
antidotes.source: EXTRIP Workgroup, Gabapentin and Pregabalin recommendations, 2022

antidotes.stem: A patient with advanced chronic kidney disease develops coma and respiratory depression after taking a therapeutic dose of baclofen. The presentation is attributed to baclofen accumulation.
antidotes.explain: EXTRIP suggests extracorporeal treatment for **baclofen toxicity in kidney impairment**, particularly when coma requires mechanical ventilation.
wrong: Flumazenil
Baclofen acts at GABA-B receptors; flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines.
Naloxone
This does not reverse baclofen toxicity.
Physostigmine
It is not an antidote for baclofen poisoning.

antidotes.stem: A patient taking haloperidol develops painful torticollis and sustained upward eye deviation shortly after a dose increase. They are alert and have no fever or autonomic instability.
antidotes.explain: This is an **acute dystonic reaction**; a parenteral anticholinergic such as benztropine rapidly relieves symptoms.
wrong: Dantrolene
Used for malignant hyperthermia and sometimes neuroleptic malignant syndrome, not uncomplicated acute dystonia.
Bromocriptine
Used in neuroleptic malignant syndrome, which is not the presentation here.
Propranolol
Can help akathisia, but is not the preferred rapid treatment for acute dystonia.
antidotes.source: Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th edition

antidotes.stem: A patient who overdosed on phenelzine is severely agitated, tachycardic and hypertensive, without evidence of end-organ injury. They are being managed in a monitored resuscitation area.
antidotes.explain: Benzodiazepines are first-line for agitation and sympathetic overactivity in **MAOI poisoning**; use supportive care and manage persistent severe hypertension with specialist guidance.
wrong: Intravenous physostigmine
It is not an antidote for MAOI poisoning and may cause serious adverse effects.
Oral activated charcoal as the only treatment
It does not control agitation or cardiovascular complications and may be unsafe in an unprotected airway.
Intravenous propranolol
Beta-blockade alone can be hazardous in severe sympathomimetic toxicity.

antidotes.stem: After an increase in risperidone, a patient develops intense inner restlessness and an inability to sit still. There is no rigidity, fever or clonus.
antidotes.explain: For antipsychotic-induced **akathisia**, propranolol is a commonly recommended symptomatic treatment, alongside reviewing the causative drug.
wrong: Benztropine
More useful for acute dystonia or parkinsonism than akathisia.
Dantrolene
Used for malignant hyperthermia and sometimes neuroleptic malignant syndrome.
Cyproheptadine
Used in selected cases of serotonin toxicity, not antipsychotic-induced akathisia.
antidotes.source: American Psychiatric Association, Practice Guideline for the Treatment of Patients With Schizophrenia, 3rd edition

antidotes.stem: A patient presents early after a large colchicine overdose, with severe vomiting and abdominal pain. The ingestion is potentially life-threatening, but the patient is currently haemodynamically stable.
antidotes.right: Urgent toxicology consultation and supportive care; no established specific antidote
antidotes.explain: There is **no routinely available specific antidote** for colchicine poisoning; early specialist advice and intensive supportive management are essential.
wrong: Intravenous folinic acid
This is used as rescue for methotrexate toxicity, not colchicine poisoning.
Intravenous vitamin K
It does not reverse colchicine toxicity.
Intravenous sodium bicarbonate
It is not a specific treatment for colchicine poisoning.
